title: Sulfonylurea-induced hypoglycaemia

card.complaint: Found confused and sweaty at home

triage.note: Brought in by her daughter, who found her confused, sweaty and slurring her words at 7 am. Type 2 diabetes. Had a stomach upset yesterday and skipped dinner.

speech.impairedText: (Confused mumbling. She can’t give a clear answer. Try asking her daughter.)

appearance.text: Alert and orientated, apologising for the fuss and asking for breakfast.
Drowsy but rousable, answering simple questions.
Confused, pale and sweaty, slurred speech, not following commands consistently.
Unresponsive to voice, twitching: a generalised seizure is starting.

history.a: I found her like this at 7. She was vomiting yesterday and skipped dinner, but she still took her evening diabetes tablets.

history.q: What diabetes medicines does she take?
history.a: Metformin and gliclazide 80 mg twice a day. No insulin.
Diabetes for 15 years and blood pressure. Her doctor said her kidneys are a bit weak.

history.q: Any fits, falls or head injury?
history.a: No fits. She didn’t fall; I found her in bed.

history.q: How are you feeling? Do you know where you are?
history.a: I’m… fine… is it Tuesday? Who are you?

variants.text: Much better, thank you. I’m so embarrassed. And starving.

exam.label: Neurological
exam.text: GCS 12 (E3 V4 M5). Pupils equal and reactive. Moving all limbs, no focal weakness. Slurred speech.

exam.label: Abdomen
exam.text: Soft, mildly tender in the epigastrium.

investigations.label: Venous blood gas
investigations.text: pH 7.39, lactate 1.6 mmol/L, K⁺ 4.3 mmol/L, glucose 2.0 mmol/L.

investigations.label: Urea & electrolytes
investigations.text: Na⁺ 137, K⁺ 4.4 mmol/L, creatinine 152 µmol/L (1.7 mg/dL), eGFR 31.

harm.why: 50% glucose is highly irritant and causes phlebitis and extravasation injury. 10% or 20% glucose is preferred.

interventions.label: Glucagon 1 mg IM
interventions.feedback: Useful when IV access is difficult, but less effective in sulfonylurea-induced hypoglycaemia and when glycogen stores are depleted by poor intake.

effects.blockedSay: Nurse: “She’s too drowsy to swallow safely. That’s an aspiration risk.”

interventions.label: Long-acting carbohydrate
interventions.detail: Toast or a meal once alert

effects.blockedSay: Nurse: “She isn’t alert enough to eat yet.”

harm.why: Insulin in a hypoglycaemic patient deepens the hypoglycaemia and risks seizures, brain injury and death.

diagnoses.label: Post-ictal state after an unwitnessed seizure

dispositions.label: Admit for glucose infusion and glucose monitoring for at least 24 h
Discharge once glucose is normal and she has eaten

critical.label: Capillary glucose checked
critical.why: Check glucose in every patient with altered consciousness: Don’t Ever Forget Glucose.

critical.label: Parenteral glucose or glucagon given
critical.why: Severe hypoglycaemia with impaired consciousness needs IV glucose (or IM glucagon if there is no IV access).

penalties.why: CT head was requested before checking glucose. Always check glucose first in altered consciousness.
Oral glucose was attempted in a patient too drowsy to swallow safely.

teaching: Check capillary glucose in every patient with altered consciousness, seizure or focal neurology.

Hypoglycaemia is glucose < 4.0 mmol/L (72 mg/dL). If the patient cannot swallow safely, give IV glucose: 150–200 mL of 10% or 75–100 mL of 20% over about 15 minutes. Use IM glucagon 1 mg if there is no IV access.
Recheck glucose 10–15 minutes after treatment and repeat treatment if it is still low.
Sulfonylureas (for example gliclazide), especially with kidney impairment, cause prolonged and recurrent hypoglycaemia: admit, run a glucose infusion and monitor for at least 24 hours.
Review the diabetes regimen before discharge, including sick-day rules.
references: Joint British Diabetes Societies for Inpatient Care. The hospital management of hypoglycaemia in adults with diabetes mellitus (current revision).
